newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Europe's economic recovery curbed by EMU.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Europe's economic recovery curbed by EMU.

text.p: European economies will revive in 1997 but will continue to pay a hefty price for toiling to meet the strict fiscal criteria of a single currency.

While the criteria will be tantalisingly close for core European countries as inflation and interest rates stay low, analysts said growth will be modest, unemployment will stay high and consumers will remain reluctant to spend.
The overall picture will be of a mild economic rebound, fuelled by a brighter business climate and improved exports, with Britain leading the pack and Italy trailing behind.

"Most of the major economies like Germany and France will grow more quickly next year," said Alex Bannister, international economist at Oxford Economic Forecasting. "But it's still going to be fairly mediocre growth."
LOW RATES BEGIN TO COUNTERACT GOVERNMENT AUSTERITY

The drive towards European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), set to begin in 1999, has been a factor behind poor economic performances of 1996 as governments slashed spending and borrowing to meet a three percent deficit to GDP target.
But looser monetary policy should begin to counteract government austerity in 1997, feeding through to business investment and pushing up growth, analysts said.
A weaker mark against the dollar and a receptive North American economy will continue to boost exports, the one bright spot of European economies in 1996.
"Monetary policy is very accomodative and should support the investment sector," Francesco Giordano, senior economist at San Paolo Bank in London, said.

Forecasts vary, but economists see German growth rising to to around 2.3 percent in 1997 from around 1.5 percent this year. France was seen posting growth of around 2.3 percent compared with around 1.3 percent this year.
Belgian growth is unlikely to get much past two percent from 1.5 percent this year, while growth in the Netherlands should continue to accelerate, hitting around 2.75 percent next year.
BRITAIN AND ITALY TO DIVERGE
Britain, further into economic recovery than continental Europe, will rebound more smartly than the others and, unlike the rest of Europe, growth will be spurred largely by consumers.
"The driving force is the UK," said Paul Horne, international economist at Smith Barney in Paris. He forecasts UK GDP at 3.3 percent in 1997 versus 2.4 percent this year.

While the strength of sterling poses a new threat for the recovering manufacturing sector, tax cuts, windfall gains, and falling unemployment will recharge consumer confidence, particularly after a general election, analysts said.
The picture is different for Italy and Spain though, with interest rates still high compared with the rest of Europe.

"There is a danger non-core countries, particularly the southern European countries, will lag behind," said Giordano. He expects growth in Italy to be around 1.2-1.5 percent next year, up from only about one percent this year.
Although interest rates in Italy and Spain will probably be cut substantially next year to stoke growth, the pressure will be on to stop cutting at the first glimmer of growth.
INTEREST RATES TO HIT BOTTOM AND STAY THERE
The German Bundesbank will set the pace for credit policy in much of Europe, with interest rates expected to stay generally low, analysts said.
The German repo rate is currently 3.0 percent. Some analysts said it could be trimmed slightly but many do not see it moving much higher in 1997.
"We think it is accomodative enough, particularly if one looks also at developments in the currency market," said Giordano, speaking of the meeker mark.
Belgian, Dutch and Austrian interest rates are all near rock bottom though there is likely to be further cutting in France, Sweden, Italy and Spain, analysts said.

The exception will be Britain, where there is speculation interest rates, currently at 6.0 percent, will need to be pushed higher to limit the consumer upswing and inflation that has a reputation for running away with itself.
MINIMAL INFLATION, HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
Elsewhere, inflation is likely to remain negligible, despite loose monetary policy, as high unemployment continues to hobble consumers.

Economists expect German unemployment to ease to around 10.1 percent next year from 10.3 percent this year. But the rate in France, which hit a record of 12.6 percent in October will edge up painfully to 13.0 percent by next spring, according to the French statistics institute.
Italy will also continue to see unemployment above 12 percent while Spain's legendary jobless rate will stay above 20 percent, analysts said.
David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Sterns in London, said, "We've got very high structural unemployment in Europe of 11.5 percent with 21 million people unemployed."
EMU WITHIN GRASP FOR SOME...BUT AT A COST
Austerity measures should bring core European economies within a whisker of meeting at least some of the EMU criteria.
Forecasts for Germany's debt to deficit ratio range from around 3.2 to 3.0 percent, while the Netherlands, Belgium, and Austria are all seen meeting or beating the target.
France, however, will struggle to meet the criteria while Italy and Spain have no chance of hitting it, forecasters say.
And that is assuming growth will improve. Some analysts say austerity measures will prove too heavy to bear.

"The massive austerity package the government has proposed will hit the (Italian) economy hard in 1997, knocking almost one full percentage point off growth despite an anticipated recovery in business confidence as interest rates fall," said IBJ.

Bear Stern's David Brown said, "From northern Scandanavia to southern Europe, everybody is squeezing themselves into this three percent budget deficit. It's producing overrestrictive policy arrangements and growth is going to slow down."
